title: Xanthe and the Wardrobe
premise: Emrys Reyes, a court translator who has spent twenty years letting their childhood language erode word by borrowed word, hears a song on a late-night radio program—a song their mother wrote and never recorded, sung in a dialect the state once punished. The broadcast leads them back to the village of their birth, to an aunt who kept the old photographs, and to the stranger standing beside their mother in every one of them: the informer whose testimony sent the singers away, and who has spent decades quietly atoning as the village's unofficial archivist. As Emrys translates the recovered songs for a dying witness who can no longer speak the language, they must decide whether justice means exposure or remembrance, and whether the person they most need to forgive is the stranger in the photographs or the child who survived by forgetting. The book ends with Emrys recording the last song in their own voice—imperfect, half-lost, but finally theirs—while choosing not to name the informer to the tribunal, and instead burying the evidence beside the mother's grave.
about_author: Casper Amberdale is the pen name of a former interpreter who worked in asylum courts for a decade before turning to fiction. They write about language, silence, and the small treasons of survival from a coastal town whose name they decline to publish.

chapters.title: The Borrowed Word
chapters.summary: Emrys, translating a custody hearing, reaches for a childhood word for 'home' and finds it gone, substituting the state language without anyone noticing. That night they inventory their mother's remaining songs in a notebook they never show anyone. POV: Emrys. Beat: the quiet horror of losing a language by consent, one convenient word at a time.

chapters.title: Static
chapters.summary: Driving home at 2 a.m., Emrys hears a folk song on a pirate-frequency broadcast—melody and verses they know, because their mother sang it and swore it was never recorded. They pull over, record it on their phone, hands shaking. POV: Emrys. Beat: the past breaching the present; wonder curdled with dread.

chapters.title: Almost Saying It
chapters.summary: A flashback chapter: nine-year-old Emrys learning at school that their language marks them, and beginning to translate for their mother at official appointments, softening what she says. POV: Emrys, past tense. Beat: the origin of the art of almost saying it—survival as the first betrayal.

chapters.title: The Archivist of Kell Hollow
chapters.summary: Emrys traces the broadcast to a retired schoolteacher, Dara Voss, who hosts an illegal heritage hour from her kitchen. Dara plays the song from a cassette labeled in handwriting Emrys almost recognizes. POV: Emrys. Beat: first ally, first door opening; the thrill and fear of being known.

chapters.title: Photographs
chapters.summary: Dara shows Emrys an album of village photographs from before the purges. In every image of the singers, a young man stands at the edge of frame, half-turned away. Emrys's mother's face is bright in three of them. POV: Emrys. Beat: the stranger enters the story; grief sharpened into a question.

chapters.title: The Aunt Who Kept the Door
chapters.summary: Emrys travels to Kell Hollow and is met by Aunt Sef, who has not spoken to them in twenty years. Sef feeds them, interrogates them, and refuses, flatly, to say the stranger's name. POV: Emrys. Beat: homecoming as ambush; love expressed as obstruction.

chapters.title: Sef's Version
chapters.summary: Sef's POV chapter: she remembers the arrests, the trial she attended as a girl, and the man who testified—Tomas Ilves, the schoolmaster's son. She also remembers what he did afterward: carrying water to prisoners' families for thirty years. Beat: the reader learns the informer's name and his long, unasked-for penance.

chapters.title: The Witness Who Forgets Forward
chapters.summary: Emrys meets Old Neni, the last living singer, now losing her memory in reverse—fluent only in the childhood tongue Emrys is losing in the opposite direction. Neni mistakes Emrys for her mother. POV: Emrys. Beat: two eroding languages meeting; tenderness and urgency fused.

chapters.title: Translation as Testimony
chapters.summary: Emrys begins daily sessions transcribing Neni's songs, discovering the lyrics are coded testimony—names, dates, the location of a mass grave the state never acknowledged. POV: Emrys. Beat: the songs stop being nostalgia and become evidence; the stakes turn legal and mortal.

chapters.title: Tomas Ilves, Retired
chapters.summary: Emrys finally meets Tomas, now an old man restoring the village chapel roof, who recognizes them instantly and says only, 'You have her chin.' He neither apologizes nor defends himself. POV: Emrys. Beat: the confrontation deferred; the discomfort of meeting evil's ordinary face.

chapters.title: What the State Wanted
chapters.summary: A middle-section pivot: Emrys researches the tribunal records in the regional archive and learns the informer's testimony was coerced—Tomas's own father was the price. The neat villain dissolves. POV: Emrys. Beat: the collapse of a clean moral story; anger with nowhere clean to land.

chapters.title: The Half-Said Apology
chapters.summary: Tomas visits Sef's kitchen while Emrys is there. He and Sef conduct an entire conversation about the weather that is visibly about 1968. Emrys translates nothing and understands everything. POV: Emrys. Beat: the chapter's title made flesh; forgiveness approached sideways, in subtext.

chapters.title: Neni's Good Day
chapters.summary: On a lucid afternoon, Neni tells Emrys directly: she knew who informed, she says, and she chose to keep singing for him anyway, because 'a voice that stops is the only victory they get.' POV: Emrys. Beat: the thematic thesis delivered by the dying witness; Emrys shaken, unconvinced.

chapters.title: The Tribunal Letter
chapters.summary: A truth-and-reconciliation commission announces a final session for unresolved cases from the purges. Emrys's transcriptions qualify as new evidence. Someone—Dara?—has already submitted Emrys's name as a witness. POV: Emrys. Beat: the private archive becomes a public weapon; the clock starts.

chapters.title: Sef's Ultimatum
chapters.summary: Sef demands Emrys withdraw: naming Tomas will destroy the village's fragile peace and expose Sef's own decades of silence—she knew, and said nothing, to keep her shop and her life. POV: Sef. Beat: the ally turns adversary; Emrys sees their own survival strategies in her.

chapters.title: The Missing Tape
chapters.summary: The cassette with the clearest song—and the most explicit testimony—vanishes from Dara's kitchen. All signs point to Tomas, who has stopped appearing at the chapel. POV: Emrys. Beat: rising tension; the question of whether Tomas is destroying evidence to hide or to protect.

chapters.title: The Chapel Roof
chapters.summary: Emrys climbs to the chapel roof at dawn and finds Tomas restoring it tile by tile; the missing tape is hidden under the altar, where Tomas has been safeguarding it for years, waiting for someone who could translate it. He finally tells the whole truth of that winter. POV: Emrys. Beat: the antagonist revealed as fellow prisoner; the confrontation the book has owed.

chapters.title: Forgiving the Stranger
chapters.summary: Emrys spends a sleepless night with the photographs, finally seeing the stranger clearly: not a monster but a boy who chose his father over his neighbors and paid for it in decades of small service. They write the witness statement—and then a second document, naming no one. POV: Emrys. Beat: the climax of the inner arc; forgiveness as an act, not a feeling.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: At the tribunal, Emrys testifies to the songs, the grave, the dead singers' names—delivering justice outside the law's reach for twenty years—while declining to identify the informer, taking the tribunal's contempt in silence. POV: Emrys. Beat: the external climax; the public price of the private choice.

chapters.title: What Sef Buried
chapters.summary: Sef, moved and shamed, reveals her own cache: her sister's letters from the camps, which she never submitted because submission felt like spending the dead. She gives them to Emrys. POV: Sef. Beat: the mirror resolves; Sef's arc completes Emrys's.

chapters.title: The Recording
chapters.summary: In Neni's room, with Dara's equipment, Emrys sings the recovered songs into a microphone—their accent wrong, half the words rebuilt from context. Neni corrects them gently, then joins in on the last verse. POV: Emrys. Beat: the resolution of the language arc; imperfect voice claimed as inheritance.

chapters.title: Xanthe and the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Emrys learns the title song's origin: 'Xanthe' was their mother's secret name for herself, and the wardrobe the hiding place where the songs survived the raids. Emrys buries the unsubmitted evidence beside her grave, keeps the recordings, and stays—teaching the village's children the words they almost lost. POV: Emrys. Beat: full-circle resolution; identity chosen rather than survived.
